body_html:
Embarrassing Spanish mistakes are a rite of passage. Nearly every English speaker has announced they were pregnant when they meant embarrassed, or told a room they were “hot” in the wrong sense. These slips happen because some Spanish words look exactly like English ones, and some innocent words carry very different meanings in different countries. Here are the classics, why they happen and what to say instead, so that if you make them, at least you’ll know why everyone is smiling.

Key takeaways
  • Embarazada means pregnant. Embarrassed is avergonzado/a or me da vergüenza.
  • Excitado and estoy caliente have sexual meanings; say emocionado and tengo calor.
  • Some verbs, like coger, are fine in Spain but vulgar in much of Latin America.
  • Native speakers are usually kind about these mistakes; laugh with them.
{{toc}}

The most embarrassing Spanish mistakes

Most of these are false friends, covered in more depth in {{link:spanish-false-friends|Spanish false friends}}.

Embarazada: the classic

This is the most famous mistake of all. Embarazada looks like “embarrassed” but, as the RAE dictionary confirms, it means pregnant. To talk about embarrassment, Spanish usually uses vergüenza:

  • ¡Qué vergüenza! How embarrassing!
  • Me da vergüenza hablar en público. Speaking in public embarrasses me.
  • Estaba muy avergonzado. I was very embarrassed.
  • Qué corte or qué pena in some countries (in Colombia and Mexico, qué pena often means “how embarrassing / sorry”).

Excited, hot and other feelings

For excitement about a trip or event, use Estoy emocionado or, even more natural, ¡Qué ganas! / Tengo muchas ganas de ir. For temperature, Spanish uses tener: Tengo calor, Tengo frío. Things can be caliente (La sopa está caliente), but people saying estoy caliente are not talking about the weather. More feeling words in {{link:talking-about-feelings-in-spanish|talking about feelings in Spanish}}.

{{image:2}}

Words that change by country

Some words are perfectly innocent in one country and rude in another:

  • Coger means to take or catch in Spain (coger el autobús), but has a vulgar sexual meaning in Mexico, Argentina and much of Latin America. Use tomar or agarrar there.
  • Concha is a shell (and a sweet bread in Mexico), but is vulgar slang in Argentina and Chile.
  • Guagua is a bus in Cuba, Puerto Rico and the Canary Islands, but a baby in Chile. Not rude, just very confusing.

When in doubt, use the most neutral word. I explore regional variation in {{link:latin-american-vs-spain-spanish|Latin American vs Spain Spanish}}.

{{book:love-slowly}}

One letter, very different words

  • año (year) vs ano (anus). Always write the ñ: Feliz año, Tengo 40 años. See {{link:spanish-accent-marks|Spanish accent marks}}.
  • cansado (tired) vs casado (married): Estoy muy casado gets a laugh.
  • hambre (hunger) vs hombre (man): Tengo hombre instead of Tengo hambre is a famous slip.
  • papa (potato) vs papá (dad) vs el Papa (the Pope).
  • pez (a live fish) vs pescado (fish as food): ordering un pez at a restaurant sounds like you want a pet.

Ser vs estar slips

Some mistakes come from {{link:ser-vs-estar|ser vs estar}}: Soy aburrido means I am a boring person, while Estoy aburrido means I’m bored. Es listo means he’s clever, Está listo means he’s ready. Saying Soy aburrida at a party is honest, but probably not what you meant.

Romantic misunderstandings

Me gustas to a new colleague sounds like a declaration; use Me caes bien. And Te amo on a second date is very intense; see {{link:how-to-use-gustar|how to use gustar}} and {{link:te-quiero-vs-te-amo|te quiero vs te amo}}.

Why these mistakes happen

Most of these slips have the same cause: English and Spanish share thousands of Latin-based words, so learners reasonably assume a similar-looking word means the same thing. Usually that works, and it is one of the great advantages English speakers have (see {{link:english-spanish-cognates|English–Spanish cognates}}). The few words where it fails are exactly the ones worth memorising.

How to recover gracefully

If you make one of these mistakes, laugh. Native speakers have heard them all, and most find them charming rather than offensive. A simple ¡Ay, perdón! Quería decir… (Oops, sorry! I meant…) fixes everything. In my experience, the people who learn fastest are the ones who aren’t afraid of being a little embarrassed, or, as I once accidentally said, a little pregnant.

{{image:3}}

Try it yourself

  1. How embarrassing! (¡Qué vergüenza!)
  2. I’m so excited about the trip. (Tengo muchas ganas del viaje.)
  3. I’m really hot, can you open the window? (Tengo mucho calor, ¿puedes abrir la ventana?)
  4. I’m very tired. (Estoy muy cansado.)
  5. Happy New Year! (¡Feliz año nuevo!)

For the full collection of mistake types, see {{link:spanish-mistakes-english-speakers-make|my guide to Spanish mistakes English speakers make}}.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

Embarrassing Spanish mistakes are part of learning, and they make great stories later. Remember the big ones (embarazada, excitado, estoy caliente, constipado), watch your ñ, use neutral words in unfamiliar countries, and when you slip, laugh and carry on.

faq.q: What does embarazada mean in Spanish?
faq.a: Embarazada means pregnant, not embarrassed. To say you are embarrassed, use Qué vergüenza, Me da vergüenza or Estoy avergonzado/a.

faq.q: How do you say “I’m hot” in Spanish without sounding rude?
faq.a: Say Tengo calor. Estoy caliente usually means aroused.

faq.q: How do you say “I’m excited” in Spanish?
faq.a: Estoy emocionado/a or, more naturally, Tengo muchas ganas. Estoy excitado has a sexual meaning.
